meta.title: Tea’s Ancient Beginnings
meta.subtitle: 40 cards · two episodes of The Tea History Podcast, researched out
meta.desc: Tea in China from the Shennong legend to the eve of the Tang, in two decks of twenty cards. Deck one follows the plant and its names: Camellia sinensis and its two varieties, the Shennong story, Lu Yu and the Classic of Tea, the character tu and how it became cha, the 59 BCE servant’s contract, the tea buds found in Emperor Jing’s tomb, Linnaeus and the Assam bush, and why half the world says tea and half says cha. Deck two follows the drink through the Bronze Age and after: the Shang and their oracle bones, the Zhou, the Erya and the Guangya, tea cakes bound with rice and brewed with onion and ginger, Chan Buddhism, the seven bushes of Mount Meng, the Qin conquest of Ba and Shu, the courtier who was allowed tea instead of wine, and the rise of tribute tea. Each card carries a ten-sentence background written from the sources listed on it, and every citation links to something you can open. Where the podcast and the scholarship disagree, the cards say so.

cards.question: Whether it becomes a malty Assam, a delicate white tea or a Japanese sencha, every true tea in the world is picked from _____, a single evergreen species.
cards.answerDate: Named1753, by Carl LinnaeusPresent name1887, by Otto Kuntze
cards.abstract:
Camellia sinensis is the evergreen shrub or small tree whose leaves and leaf buds make every true tea on earth. Black, green, white, yellow, oolong and dark teas are not different plants but different treatments of the same leaf, separated by how far it is allowed to oxidise before heat stops the enzymes. Left alone the plant grows into a tree: wild specimens reach 5 metres (16 feet) and occasionally 20 metres (66 feet), while a plucking bush is kept at about a metre (3 feet) with a flat table of new shoots on top. Its leaves run from 4 to 22 centimetres (1.6 to 8.7 inches) long, and fresh ones carry roughly 4% caffeine, which the plant makes as an insecticide rather than as a favour to the drinker. Botanists trace the species to the borderlands where far eastern India, northern Myanmar and southwestern China meet, the belt that Yunnan and Sichuan sit at the edge of.

Carl Linnaeus described the plant in 1753 as Thea sinensis, having never seen a living one. In the second edition of Species Plantarum he split it in two, Thea viridis for green tea and Thea bohea for black, on the strength of an unevidenced claim by the English writer John Hill that the two came from different plants. They did not, and the error took the better part of a century and a half to unwind: Robert Sweet folded the genus Thea into Camellia in 1818, and the accepted name today credits Linnaeus and Otto Kuntze, who published the combination in 1887. Five varieties are recognised, of which two carry the world’s tea: var. sinensis, the small-leaved, cold-hardy, long-lived China bush, and var. assamica, the large-leaved, softer, subtropical Assam type. Everything else, the thousands of named cultivars and the famous mountain gardens alike, is variation worked on one species across roughly two thousand years of selection.
sources: William H. Ukers, All About Tea, 2 vols. (New York: Tea and Coffee Trade Journal Company, 1935), https://archive.org/details/allabouttea00uker.

cards.question: Chinese tradition hands the discovery of tea to _____, the Divine Farmer, who is said to have tasted a hundred plants and survived seventy-two poisons in a single day.
cards.answerDate: Traditional datec. 2700 BCEEarliest mentions3rd – 2nd century BCE
cards.abstract:
Shennong, whose name means the Divine Farmer, is one of the culture heroes of earliest Chinese tradition, sometimes counted among the Three Sovereigns beside Fuxi and the Yellow Emperor. He is credited with giving China agriculture itself, the plough and the hoe and the wells and the irrigation ditches, along with markets, herbal medicine and in some tellings the calendar. He is also called the Yan Emperor, and Chinese folk religion has venerated him continuously for more than two thousand years. The stories are not contemporary records: he first appears in texts of the third and second centuries BCE such as the Lüshi Chunqiu and the Huainanzi, and later in Sima Qian’s Shiji, all written a very long time after the age they describe. The Huainanzi gives the most famous version of his method, in which he tastes hundreds of plants and takes seventy poisons in one day to learn what each of them does.

Tea enters that story as the antidote. In the best-known telling Shennong is boiling water in the open when leaves blow down from the tree above him into the pot, and he drinks the result and finds himself refreshed. In a second version the leaves reach him as he lies poisoned and purge him; in a third he notices the scent of a tea bush burning and works backwards from the smell to the leaf. Lu Yu opened the Classic of Tea in the eighth century CE by naming Shennong as the discoverer, and it is largely through Lu Yu that the legend became the standard account. None of it is verifiable and the traditional date of about 2700 BCE sits far outside Chinese written history, but the story still matters, because it is the claim on which China’s authorship of tea has rested for twelve centuries.
sources: Laszlo Montgomery, “Ep. 1 | Tea’s Ancient Beginnings in China,” The Tea History Podcast, https://open.spotify.com/episode/0HPN8bcWGzQYC0lLYUwiNJ.

cards.question: China’s oldest surviving pharmacopoeia, the _____, sorts 365 drugs into three grades according to how safely each can be taken over a long period.
cards.answerDate: Compiled1st – 2nd century CEAttributed toShennong, c. 2700 BCE
cards.abstract:
The Shennong Bencaojing, the Divine Farmer’s Classic of Materia Medica, is the oldest surviving Chinese pharmacopoeia and the foundation of the whole later herbal tradition. It is attributed to Shennong himself, but scholars read it as a compilation of older oral and written lore assembled in the first or second century CE. It describes 365 substances drawn from minerals, plants and animals, one for each day of the year. Those are sorted into three grades: 120 upper drugs held to be harmless and fit for long use, 120 middle drugs that heal but can harm, and 125 lower drugs that are powerful or frankly poisonous. That three-grade scheme, rather than any individual remedy in it, is the book’s lasting contribution, and Chinese pharmacology worked within it for the next fifteen hundred years, adding new substances to the grades rather than replacing the grades themselves.

The original text did not survive as a book, and no manuscript of it is known. It reaches us because later compilers quoted it wholesale, above all Tao Hongjing around 500 CE, and Qing scholars reassembled it out of those quotations. Tea’s place in the work is a good deal less secure than the popular accounts of tea make it sound, and the difference turns on which book the famous sentence actually came from. The line everyone quotes, that tea tastes bitter and that drinking it makes one think faster, sleep less, move more nimbly and see more clearly, reaches us through Lu Yu, who credits it to a Shennong shijing, a Divine Farmer’s food classic that is itself lost. So the most famous early endorsement of tea is an eighth-century quotation of a book nobody has seen since, which is a fair description of nearly everything claimed about the drink before the Han.

cards.question: Raised in a Buddhist monastery and later honoured as the Sage of Tea, _____ wrote the first book in the world devoted entirely to the subject.
cards.answerDate: Born733 CEDied804 CECha Jing written760 – 762 CE
cards.abstract:
Lu Yu was a Tang writer from Tianmen in Hubei who became, and has remained, the single most important figure in the history of tea. Abandoned as an infant, he was raised at the Longgai monastery, where he was brewing tea for his elders before he had learned much else. He spent six years studying under the scholar Zou Fuzi on Mount Huomen, and was taken up by Cui Guofu, a demoted official and accomplished poet who gave him a literary education. He passed the years of the An Lushan rebellion in the tea country south of the Yangtze, walking the gardens, watching the picking and the firing, and questioning the growers and monks who did both. Out of that came the Cha Jing, the Classic of Tea, written between 760 and 762 CE.

Chinese tradition calls him the Cha Sheng, the Sage of Tea, and puts him in a class of his own among the many later writers on the subject. Tea merchants made pottery figures of him and treated him as a household god of the trade, which is an unusual afterlife for an author. His influence was practical as much as literary: he set out what equipment tea needed, which water suited it, how a cake should be roasted and ground, and what the finished bowl ought to look like. He wrote a second work on tea as well, the Hui Chalun, which did as much as the first to spread the habit of drinking it, along with poetry and local history. He died in 804 CE, by which time tea had travelled from a southwestern curiosity to an everyday drink of the Tang empire, and one the state had begun to think worth taxing.

cards.question: Lu Yu’s _____ runs to about 7,000 characters in ten chapters covering the plant, the tools, the water, the brewing and the regions that grow it.
cards.answerDate: Written760 – 762 CEOldest editionsMing, 1368 – 1644 CE
cards.abstract:
The Cha Jing, or Classic of Tea, is the first book anywhere in the world written entirely about tea, and it has never quite been displaced. Lu Yu composed it between 760 and 762 CE, in roughly 7,000 characters of compressed Tang prose. It was issued as three scrolls holding ten chapters, with chapters one to three in the first scroll, chapter four alone in the second, and chapters five to ten in the third. The ten take the subject in order: the plant and its origins, the tools for picking and pressing, the making, the vessels, the boiling, the drinking, the historical record, the growing regions, what may be left out when travelling, and how the whole should be written on a scroll. After the Tang the three scrolls were combined into one book and the original arrangement dropped out of circulation.

The first chapter is where the Shennong legend became the standard account of tea’s origin, because Lu Yu put it at the head of everything that followed. The seventh chapter gathers earlier references to tea out of texts that in several cases no longer survive anywhere else, which makes the book a primary source for works it does no more than quote. Lu Yu’s own manuscript is long gone and the earliest surviving editions are Ming. What the book did was turn a medicinal decoction into a practice with standards attached to it: the right water, the right heat, the right vessel and the right taste, each of them argued for rather than asserted. Every Chinese treatise on tea written since has stood in its shadow, and the Japanese tea ceremony traces its own ancestry back through it to the Tang.
sources: William H. Ukers, All About Tea, 2 vols. (New York: Tea and Coffee Trade Journal Company, 1935), https://archive.org/details/allabouttea00uker.

cards.question: Before the character cha settled into general use, Chinese texts wrote tea as _____, a character that also named a bitter herb and caused centuries of confusion.
cards.answerDate: Used for teabefore c. 725 CESuperseded by cha8th century CE
cards.abstract:
Tu, written 荼, is the character that stood for tea in Chinese writing through most of the period before the Tang. It is the character cha 茶 carrying one extra horizontal stroke, and the two are easy to mistake for one another on a page. Cha was in fact derived from it, by dropping that stroke, at some point around the eighth century CE. The difficulty for historians is that tu was never a word for tea alone: it also named a bitter herb or vegetable, usually identified with the sow thistle, and known in Chinese as kucai. So every occurrence of the character in an early text, in the Book of Songs or the Book of Rites, has to be read in context to decide which plant is meant, and scholars have argued over individual passages for centuries.

What the ambiguity says about the drink is worth noticing, because the same word served for tea and for something eaten precisely because it was bitter. The Erya glosses the tea word jia as ku tu, bitter tu, which is a deliberate identification rather than an accident of spelling. Tu was not the only early name for the leaf either. Chinese sources list several, among them jia, she, ming and chuan, most of which are credited to the people of Sichuan, and it took until the Tang for one of them to win outright. Fujian never quite got the message and went on using tu, pronounced in the local Min speech as something close to te, which is the reason much of Europe says tea rather than cha.
sources: Laszlo Montgomery, “Ep. 1 | Tea’s Ancient Beginnings in China,” The Tea History Podcast, https://open.spotify.com/episode/0HPN8bcWGzQYC0lLYUwiNJ.

cards.question: A Western Han contract of 59 BCE known as the _____ orders a bought servant to boil tea, wash the vessels afterwards and buy tea at Wuyang.
cards.answerDate: Written59 BCEAuthorWang Bao, died c. 61 BCE
cards.abstract:
The Tongyue, usually rendered as the Contract for a Youth or the Slave’s Contract, is a short satirical document written by the Shu poet Wang Bao in 59 BCE. It is framed as the deed of sale for a servant named Bianliao, bought from a Lady Yang Hui of Chengdu, and it lists in exhausting detail everything the man is henceforth obliged to do. The joke is the sheer length of the list, which runs from ploughing and weaving to catching birds and hauling water until no hour of the day has been left unaccounted for. It is also, incidentally, one of the most useful economic documents to survive from the Western Han, because a writer inventing a joke about chores has no reason to invent the wrong ones. Two of the chores on it concern tea, and they are the reason a minor piece of Han humour is quoted in every history of the drink.

The servant is to boil tea and clean the utensils afterwards, and he is to travel to Wuyang to buy tea. That is the earliest datable written reference to tea being prepared as a drink, and it places the practice in Sichuan a century and a half before the common era. Wuyang, a town not far from Chengdu, is accordingly the first tea market anywhere on record, and Wang Bao, a native of Shu, thought its leaf the best to be had. The document also shows tea being bought rather than gathered, which implies growers, a market price and a trade already working in the second half of the first century BCE. For two thousand years the Tongyue was the earliest hard evidence for tea in China, and it held that position until leaves were identified in an imperial tomb and published in 2016.
sources: Houyuan Lu et al., “Earliest tea as evidence for one branch of the Silk Road across the Tibetan Plateau,” Scientific Reports 6 (2016): 18955, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep18955.

cards.question: Archaeologists working through the burial pits of the _____ outside Xi’an identified tea buds that had lain in the ground since about 141 BCE.
cards.answerDate: Tomb sealed141 BCETea published2016
cards.abstract:
The Yangling Mausoleum, Han Yangling, is the tomb complex of Emperor Jing of Han and his empress, standing north of modern Xi’an in Shaanxi province. It is ringed by scores of burial pits packed with the emperor’s household in miniature, including some 40,000 pottery figures along with animals, chariots, granaries and stores of real food. Those pits are what make the site useful beyond its architecture, because they were furnished with genuine goods as well as with models of them, and organic material survived in several. Among the material lifted out of them was a quantity of small, tightly packed plant remains that resisted identification for years after they were excavated. In 2016 a team led by Houyuan Lu published the answer in Scientific Reports.

The remains were tea, and they were made almost entirely of buds rather than mature leaves, which is to say a fine tea rather than a rough one. The identification rested on two lines of evidence drawn from the material itself, the biomolecular traces the leaf leaves behind and the phytoliths, the microscopic silica bodies that form inside a living leaf and keep their shape long after everything organic has gone. Because Emperor Jing died in 141 BCE and the pits were sealed at his burial, the leaves are at least 2,100 years old. That makes them the oldest tea so far identified anywhere in the world. The same paper reported tea of comparable age from Ngari in western Tibet, which puts the leaf on a Himalayan branch of the Silk Road by the second or third century CE, several hundred years earlier than any previous evidence allowed.
sources: Houyuan Lu et al., “Earliest tea as evidence for one branch of the Silk Road across the Tibetan Plateau,” Scientific Reports 6 (2016): 18955, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep18955.

cards.question: The tea found at Yangling was sealed in the ground for _____, the ruler who crushed the Rebellion of the Seven States and fathered Emperor Wu.
cards.answerDate: Born188 BCEReigned157 – 141 BCEDied141 BCE
cards.abstract:
Emperor Jing of Han, personal name Liu Qi, was the sixth emperor of the Han dynasty and reigned from 157 to 141 BCE. He inherited from his father, Emperor Wen, a state deliberately run on light taxes and a light hand, and he continued the policy. The two reigns together are remembered as the Rule of Wen and Jing, treated in Chinese historiography as one of the golden ages, and shaped by the quietist political thinking of the Daoists. The great crisis of his own reign came in 154 BCE, when seven princely states rose against him after he moved to cut their territories back. His generals starved the rebellion out by cutting its supply lines, and the princes never again held independent power worth the name.

What that victory bought was a centralised state, and it was his son Emperor Wu who spent the proceeds on conquest and on the Silk Road. Jing was buried in 141 BCE at Yangling, north of the capital, in a tomb ringed with the pits of pottery figures and household provisions that make the site so unusually informative. Those provisions included tea, sealed in with him at the burial and then unrecognised for the better part of two decades after the pits were opened. His tomb is therefore the earliest point at which tea can be tied to a named person, a fixed place and a firm year rather than to a legend or to a literary joke. The leaves also say something about who drank it: an emperor was being supplied with buds alone, so tea was already graded, and a fine grade already existed to be reserved for him.
sources: Houyuan Lu et al., “Earliest tea as evidence for one branch of the Silk Road across the Tibetan Plateau,” Scientific Reports 6 (2016): 18955, https://doi.org/10.1038/srep18955.

cards.question: The binomial system that eventually gave tea the name Camellia sinensis was set out by _____, the Swedish naturalist who named the tea plant from dried material and travellers’ reports.
cards.answerDate: Born1707Died1778Species Plantarum1753
cards.abstract:
Carl Linnaeus was the Swedish naturalist who gave biology the system of two-part Latin names it still uses. Before him a species was described by a Latin phrase that could run to a dozen words and varied from author to author; after him it had a genus and a specific epithet and nothing else. He set the method out for plants in Species Plantarum in 1753 and for animals in the tenth edition of Systema Naturae in 1758, and both are taken as the starting points of modern nomenclature. He worked largely from dried specimens sent home by correspondents and by the travelling collectors he called his apostles, several of whom died on the journey. Tea was one of the plants he wanted most and could least easily obtain, and he leaned on Swedish East India Company captains such as Carl Gustaf Ekeberg, who made ten voyages to India and China and brought him reports of the tea tree.

In 1753 he named it Thea sinensis, tea of China, working from material and reports rather than from the plant. In the second edition he divided it into Thea viridis and Thea bohea, a green-tea species and a black-tea species, following the English writer John Hill. That was wrong, and the mistake is a fair illustration of the limits of the method: a European market distinction had been read back into the plant. It took until the nineteenth century for botanists to accept that green and black tea are the same leaf differently handled. The genus Thea was folded into Camellia in 1818, and the name the plant carries today still credits Linnaeus for the epithet he chose in 1753.

cards.question: Linnaeus set out two-part Latin names for the whole known plant world in _____, the 1753 work that botany still treats as its starting point.
cards.answerDate: Published1753Second edition1762 – 1763
cards.abstract:
Species Plantarum is the book in which Carl Linnaeus described every plant species then known to European science, published in two volumes in 1753. It covers about 7,300 species, arranged by his sexual system, which sorted plants by the number and arrangement of their stamens and pistils. Its importance is not the arrangement, which was frankly artificial and was abandoned within a century, but the names it carried in its margins. In the margin beside each long descriptive phrase Linnaeus wrote a single word, and that word with the genus name in front of it made a two-part label any botanist anywhere could use. Botanical nomenclature is formally dated from the first of May 1753, the book’s publication date, so a plant name printed before it has no standing at all and cannot be revived.

Tea appears in the first edition as Thea sinensis, in a genus of its own that Linnaeus had erected for it alone. Linnaeus had no living plant to work from and was relying on dried material, drawings and the accounts of sailors and merchants who had seen the gardens. By the second edition, printed in 1762 and 1763, he had split the entry into Thea viridis and Thea bohea, a green species and a black one, after the English writer John Hill asserted without evidence that they were different plants. Bohea is itself a European mangling of Wuyi, the Fujian mountains whose dark teas dominated the early trade, so a shipping term had become a species. Both of those names were eventually abandoned and the plant moved into the genus Camellia, but the epithet sinensis that Linnaeus chose in 1753 has stayed attached to tea ever since, and is the oldest part of its name.
sources: William H. Ukers, All About Tea, 2 vols. (New York: Tea and Coffee Trade Journal Company, 1935), https://archive.org/details/allabouttea00uker.

cards.question: The large, soft-leaved tea of the hot subtropical valleys, the plant behind most strong black tea, is the variety _____, named after the Indian province.
cards.answerDate: Wild tea reportedAssam, c. 1823IdentifiedCalcutta, early 1830s
cards.abstract:
Camellia sinensis var. assamica is the large-leaved form of the tea plant, one of the two varieties that between them supply nearly all the world’s tea. Its leaves are bigger and softer than those of the China bush and can reach the upper end of the species range, above 20 centimetres (8 inches). Left unpruned it is frankly a tree rather than a shrub, and wild specimens are the ones that reach 20 metres (66 feet). It wants heat and a great deal of rain, thrives in subtropical monsoon country, and is markedly less hardy in cold than its Chinese relative. Its leaf oxidises readily and yields the brisk, malty, strongly coloured liquor that most of the world means when it says black tea, a character the Assam monsoon and its heat do much to produce.

The variety takes its name from Assam in northeastern India, where the Scottish trader Robert Bruce was shown tea growing wild by the Singpho people around 1823, who were already brewing the leaves themselves. Bruce died before the plant could be classified, his brother Charles sent leaves and seeds to the botanical garden at Calcutta in the early 1830s, and what mattered commercially was that the assumption that tea could only come out of China had been broken. The Java bush, sometimes given as a third type, is this same Assam plant carried to Indonesia, and is usually treated as var. cambodiensis or folded back into assamica. Assamica is also the plant of the old Yunnan tea forests, which is the geographical point behind the botany: the two varieties meet along the Yunnan and upper Myanmar frontier. Pu-erh, the dark compressed tea of Yunnan, is made from it, which ties the variety back to the region where the whole story began.
sources: Laszlo Montgomery, “Ep. 1 | Tea’s Ancient Beginnings in China,” The Tea History Podcast, https://open.spotify.com/episode/0HPN8bcWGzQYC0lLYUwiNJ.

cards.question: The small-leaved, cold-hardy and unusually long-lived form of the tea plant, grown for green and white teas, is the variety _____, the type variety of the species and the one Europe met first.
cards.answerDate: Named1753, by Carl LinnaeusVarieties5 in the species
cards.abstract:
Camellia sinensis var. sinensis is the China bush, the small-leaved form of the tea plant and the one that Europeans met first. Its leaves are at the short end of the species range and its bushes are naturally smaller than the Assam type, which is one reason it is easier to keep as a clipped hedge. It tolerates cold far better, which is why tea can be grown at altitude and as far north as it is, and individual plants are said to live a great deal longer. Its leaf oxidises more slowly and holds up better to gentle handling, so it suits green, white and yellow teas and the lighter oolongs. Almost every famous Chinese tea, Longjing and the Fujian whites among them, is made from one cultivar or another of it, and so is nearly all Japanese tea.

It is the type variety of the species, because it is the plant Linnaeus had in mind in 1753 when he coined sinensis, meaning of China. Botanically it is one of five recognised varieties of the species, the others being assamica, pubilimba, dehungensis and madoensis, of which only the first two are of any commercial account. The two commercially important varieties differ enough in habit and hardiness to be treated as separate plants by growers, and not enough to be separate species. The ranges of the two overlap in the borderland where southwestern China, northern Myanmar and far eastern India meet, which is also where the species as a whole is thought to have originated. Everything a Chinese tea garden has done for two thousand years, all the selection and grafting and naming of cultivars, has been done to this one variety.
sources: William H. Ukers, All About Tea, 2 vols. (New York: Tea and Coffee Trade Journal Company, 1935), https://archive.org/details/allabouttea00uker.

cards.question: A tea plant selected, named and propagated by growers rather than found wild is properly called a _____, a word contracted from two longer ones in 1923.
cards.answerDate: Term coined1923Coined byL. H. Bailey, 1858 – 1954
cards.abstract:
A cultivar is a plant selected and maintained by people for qualities they happen to want, and kept distinct from its neighbours by being propagated deliberately rather than left to breed freely. The word is a contraction of cultivated variety, coined by the American horticulturist Liberty Hyde Bailey in 1923. It is not the same thing as a botanical variety: a variety is a wild population a botanist recognises, while a cultivar exists because somebody kept it going. Cultivar names are governed by a code of their own and are written in single quotation marks after the species name, in ordinary roman type rather than in the italics a botanical name takes. Many are clones, raised from cuttings rather than from seed, so that every plant in a field is genetically identical to the single bush it was taken from.

Tea is an extreme case of the practice, and thousands of named tea cultivars are in cultivation across China, Japan, India and Taiwan. Chinese growers have been selecting bushes for aroma, leaf size, flush timing and cold tolerance for a very long time, and matching a cultivar to a particular hillside is part of what makes a famous tea famous. The cultivar is therefore where the botany and the taste actually meet: the species is one, the variety is one of two, and the cultivar is the thing in the cup. It also explains how two teas can taste nothing alike while a botanist goes on insisting, quite correctly, that they are the same plant. Wine growers reach for the word varietal to do roughly the same work, but in the tea world the stricter term is the usual one, and a named bush is a cultivar.

cards.question: The words cultigen and cultivar, now standard wherever cultivated plants are named, were both coined by _____, the Cornell horticulturist and botanist.
cards.answerDate: Born1858Died1954Coined cultivar1923
cards.abstract:
Liberty Hyde Bailey was an American horticulturist, botanist and reformer, and the man who gave cultivated plants a vocabulary of their own. He was born on a Michigan farm in 1858 and spent most of his working life at Cornell, where he built the college of agriculture and ran it as its first dean. He wrote or edited an extraordinary quantity of reference work, including the multi-volume Cyclopedia of American Horticulture, and he collected plants in the field into his eighties. He also chaired the Country Life Commission for President Theodore Roosevelt, and argued all his life for rural education, for the standing of farming and for what would now be called sustainability. The Liberty Hyde Bailey Hortorium at Cornell, the herbarium he founded for cultivated plants, still carries his name and his collections.

The naming problem he set out to solve was real: botanical rank was built for wild populations and fitted badly onto plants that exist only because gardeners made them. In 1923, in his journal Gentes Herbarum, he proposed cultigen for a plant whose origin lies in deliberate human activity, and cultivar, contracted from cultivated variety, for a named kind within one. Both words were taken up by horticulture, and cultivar now has an international code of nomenclature written around it, quite separate from the botanical one. For tea the consequence is direct, because the thousands of named Chinese and Japanese tea bushes are cultivars in exactly Bailey’s sense: they exist because growers kept selecting and propagating them. He died in 1954 at the age of ninety-six, having spent seventy years insisting that plants people grow deserved as much rigour as plants they find.
sources: Laszlo Montgomery, “Ep. 1 | Tea’s Ancient Beginnings in China,” The Tea History Podcast, https://open.spotify.com/episode/0HPN8bcWGzQYC0lLYUwiNJ.

cards.question: Xu Shen’s _____, presented to the throne in 121 CE, analysed more than 9,000 characters and organised them under 540 graphic headings.
cards.answerDate: Compiledc. 100 CEPresented121 CEEntries9,353 characters
cards.abstract:
The Shuowen Jiezi is the first Chinese dictionary to take a character apart and explain how it was built, rather than simply glossing what it means. Xu Shen finished it around 100 CE and it was presented to Emperor An of the Eastern Han in 121 CE. It treats 9,353 characters plus 1,163 graphic variants, running to some 133,000 characters of text in all. Xu Shen’s innovation was to file every character under one of 540 shared graphic components, an ancestor of the radical system every Chinese dictionary has used since. He also set out the six categories of character formation, among them pictographs, simple indicatives, compound indicatives and the phono-semantic compounds that make up the great bulk of the writing system.

Tea is in it, entered under the name ming rather than cha, and described as the buds picked from the tu plant. That short gloss is more useful than it looks, because it shows that by the early second century CE the Chinese had worked out that the buds were the part worth taking, and that plucking them makes the bush throw more. Two thousand years later the most expensive green and white teas in China are still made of buds alone, which is the same judgement arrived at twice with a great deal of history in between. The Han text itself did not survive as an object: the oldest fragment anyone has is Tang, and it amounts to roughly two per cent of the whole work. What is read today descends from the Song editions of the brothers Xu Xuan and Xu Kai, whose work of the 980s is why the dictionary exists at all.

cards.question: One of the several early Chinese names for tea, still used as a literary word for it today, is _____, which the Shuowen Jiezi glosses as buds of the tu plant.
cards.answerDate: In the Shuowen121 CEIn Guo Pu’s Eryac. 310 CE
cards.abstract:
Ming, written 茗, is one of the handful of names the Chinese used for tea in the centuries before the character cha won out over all of them. Lu Yu lists it in the Classic of Tea among the several names the leaf had gone by, alongside cha, jia, she and chuan, and treats all of them as words for one thing. Most of those names are credited by the Chinese sources to the people of Sichuan, which is consistent with everything else known about where the drinking of tea actually started. What ming actually denoted is not entirely settled, however, and the two earliest sources to define it pull in exactly opposite directions. Xu Shen’s Shuowen Jiezi of 121 CE explains it as the buds picked from the tu plant, which makes it the fine, early-plucked material.

Guo Pu’s commentary on the Erya, written around 310 CE, says instead that leaves gathered late are called ming, which makes it the coarse end. Both readings survive in later usage, the disagreement has never been fully resolved, and it is a good illustration of how little the surviving record really pins down about early tea. What is clear is that the word did not die when cha took over the everyday register of the language. Ming survived instead as the literary and poetic word for tea, and it is still there in compounds that a modern reader will meet on the sign above a tea shop. It is a useful corrective to the tidy story of one name simply replacing another, since several words for the leaf were plainly in circulation at the same time for centuries on end.
sources: Laszlo Montgomery, “Ep. 1 | Tea’s Ancient Beginnings in China,” The Tea History Podcast, https://open.spotify.com/episode/0HPN8bcWGzQYC0lLYUwiNJ.

cards.question: Because Dutch traders bought their first cargoes in Fujian, where _____ is spoken, most of western Europe calls the drink tea rather than cha.
cards.answerDate: Dutch importsfrom c. 1606Cha replaces tu8th century CE
cards.abstract:
Hokkien is the Min Nan speech of southern Fujian, the province that faced the sea and did most of China’s early business with foreign merchants. Its word for tea is te, and that single syllable is the reason for one of the neatest and most often noticed patterns in the vocabulary of the world’s languages. Almost every language on earth calls the drink by a word descended either from te or from cha, and which of the two it uses is a record of how the tea first reached its speakers. Mandarin and Cantonese both say cha, and that form travelled overland with the caravans of the Silk Road into Central Asia, Persia, Turkey, Russia and much of India. Portuguese traders working around Canton and Macau from the 1550s took that southern cha home with them, and Portuguese still says chá where its neighbours do not.

The Dutch bought in Fujian instead, shipping their first tea around 1606 by way of Macau, Bantam and Java, and what they heard from their suppliers was te. They carried it home as thee, and because the Dutch East India Company dominated the early European trade, their pronunciation went with the cargo. English tea, French thé, German Tee, Italian tè and Spanish té all descend from that one Fujianese syllable. There is a Chinese reason behind the split as well as a European one: when cha replaced tu as the standard written word around the eighth century, Fujian carried on with the older form. So the accident that fixed the word in half the world’s languages was a province declining to change its habits a thousand years before the Dutch turned up.

cards.question: The southwestern province of _____ holds China’s oldest tea trees and is where, by long tradition, the cultivation of the plant began.
cards.answerDate: Old tea forests10th century onwardsJingmai inscribed2023
cards.abstract:
Yunnan is the mountainous province of China’s far southwest, bordering Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam, and it sits at the heart of the region where tea is thought to have originated. The old primeval tea forest, before modern frontiers cut it into pieces, ran from Sichuan and Yunnan across the hills of northern Myanmar, Thailand and Laos and on into Assam and northern Vietnam. The soil, the rainfall and the altitude suited the plant, and in that belt tea grows as a tree rather than a bush. That is the practical trouble with wild tea, because the leaves are up among the branches and a picker has to climb the tree to reach any of them. Over the centuries most tea trees were felled and replaced with waist-high bushes that could be picked standing up, which is far cheaper in labour if not in character.

Yunnan is the great exception, and ancient trees survive there in groves that are still picked commercially rather than kept as curiosities. The forests of Jingmai Mountain in Pu’er, tended by the Blang and Dai peoples since roughly the tenth century, cover about 1,180 hectares of old tea forest around nine villages. UNESCO added that cultural landscape to the World Heritage List in 2023, recognising a system of agroforestry in which tea is grown under the forest canopy rather than in cleared plantations. Yunnan’s tea is the large-leaved assamica variety, and it is the raw material of pu-erh, the dark compressed tea the province is known for. Claims about individual trees being one, two or three thousand years old are made very often and verified very rarely, so any particular figure of that kind is worth treating with care.

cards.question: The two-volume survey All About Tea, published in 1935 and still quoted constantly, was the work of _____, an American trade journalist.
cards.answerDate: Born1873Died1945All About Tea1935
cards.abstract:
William H. Ukers was an American trade journalist who wrote the two books that dominated English-language writing on tea and coffee for most of the twentieth century. He was born William Harrison Ukers in 1873 and began as an editor on The Spice Mill, the house magazine of a coffee-roasting firm. In 1901, after an idea of his for expanding it was turned down, he left and founded the Tea and Coffee Trade Journal, which he then edited for the rest of his working life. All About Coffee came first, in 1922, and remains the better known of the two outside the tea business. All About Tea followed in 1935, published by his own journal company in two volumes running to well over a thousand pages.

It attempts the whole subject: botany, the history of every producing country, cultivation, manufacture, transport, markets, advertising, a chronology, a dictionary of tea terms and a long bibliography. The scale is what makes it valuable, because Ukers gathered material that had never been collected in English and in some cases has not been collected since. It is also a book of its moment, written from inside the trade and from an imperial vantage point, and its account of the original wild tea forests is a description of a region already being carved into nation states. Later scholarship has corrected a good deal of it, particularly on the early Chinese sources, so it is best treated as a first stop and a rich quarry rather than as a last word. Ukers died in 1945, and both books have been reprinted, quoted and argued with ever since, the tea volume as recently as 2007.

cards.question: The first Chinese dynasty confirmed by its own written records is the _____, whose scribes cut divinations into ox bones and turtle shells at Anyang.
cards.answerDate: Ruledc. 1600 – 1046 BCELate capitalAnyang, from c. 1250 BCE
cards.abstract:
The Shang dynasty ruled the North China Plain from about 1600 to 1046 BCE and is the earliest Chinese dynasty for which there is direct written evidence. That evidence is the oracle bones, and until they were recognised in 1899 many scholars treated the Shang as legendary in the way the Xia still largely is. Its heartland lay along the Yellow River in what is now Henan, and its last capital stood at Anyang from roughly 1250 BCE. Shang bronze casting was the most accomplished in the world at the time, producing ritual vessels of a technical quality nobody else approached for centuries. The state was held together by kinship, by divination and by war, and the evidence from its royal tombs shows it practising human sacrifice on a considerable scale.

Tea is nowhere in the Shang record at all, and that absence is worth stating plainly rather than reading around. No character for it appears on the oracle bones or on the bronzes, because the plant grew in the far southwest and Shang civilisation was a northern affair. The claim that tea was sent north as tribute in Shang times rests on much later texts rather than on anything contemporary. The best of those, the fourth-century Huayang Guozhi, describes the rulers of Ba sending tea along with lacquer and honey to King Wu of Zhou, which is to say at the very end of the Shang or just after it. The honest position is that tea was very probably being gathered and used in the southwest while the Shang ruled the north, and that the Shang themselves left no trace whatever of knowing about it.

cards.question: The earliest substantial body of Chinese writing is _____, incised on ox shoulder blades and turtle plastrons that were heated until they cracked.
cards.answerDate: In usec. 1250 – 1046 BCERecognised1899
cards.abstract:
Oracle bone script is the writing the Shang kings used to record divination, and it is the oldest substantial Chinese writing known. A diviner put a question to the ancestors, applied heat to a prepared ox scapula or turtle plastron until it cracked, read the cracks, and had the question and sometimes the outcome cut into the bone beside them. The questions put to them are overwhelmingly practical: harvests, weather, illness, childbirth, hunting, the correct sacrifice to make, and whether a campaign would end well. The script is already mature, with several thousand distinct characters and the same principles of formation that Chinese uses today, so it is plainly not the beginning of writing in China but the earliest part of it that survives. Roughly 150,000 inscribed pieces have been recovered, the great majority from Yinxu at Anyang.

They came to scholarly notice in 1899, when it was realised that the dragon bones being ground up and sold as medicine in Beijing carried ancient writing on them. What the bones did for history was to confirm a king list: the Shang rulers named in them match those Sima Qian recorded more than a thousand years later. For the history of tea their significance is entirely negative, which is the kind of evidence easiest to overlook and often the most telling. A corpus this large, this concerned with crops and offerings, and this early would show tea if the Shang court had known it, and it does not. The knowledge of the leaf stayed south of the Yangtze for several centuries more, which is why the written history of tea begins so much later than the plant does.

cards.question: The last Shang capital, excavated near Anyang since 1928 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2006, is known as _____, the Ruins of Yin.
cards.answerDate: Capitalc. 1250 – 1046 BCEExcavatedfrom 1928Inscribed2006
cards.abstract:
Yinxu, the Ruins of Yin, is the site of the last Shang capital, on the Huan River at Anyang in northern Henan. It served as the seat of the Shang kings from about 1250 BCE until the dynasty fell in 1046 BCE, and it is one of the largest and oldest archaeological sites in China. Systematic excavation began in 1928 under Li Ji, the first Chinese archaeologist trained in the modern discipline, and it has continued with interruptions ever since. The site has yielded palace and temple foundations, royal tombs, bronze foundries, chariot burials and the great bulk of the oracle bone corpus. Its single most famous find is the tomb of Fu Hao, discovered unlooted in 1976 and dated to about 1250 BCE, the burial of a consort of King Wu Ding who commanded armies in her own right.

Yinxu matters out of all proportion to its size because it settled an argument that had been running for a very long time. Before it, the Shang were known only from texts written a thousand years and more after the fact, and a good many historians both Chinese and foreign doubted that the dynasty had existed at all. UNESCO inscribed the site on the World Heritage List in 2006, on the strength of exactly that contribution to the written history of the country. For the history of tea the site is a very large piece of negative evidence, since nothing in this enormous northern archive mentions the leaf. Anyang sits on the Yellow River and the tea forests lay a thousand kilometres (620 miles) and more to the southwest, which is the whole of the explanation.

cards.question: The last Shang ruler, remembered for a pool of wine and a forest of hung meat, is _____, though the charges against him were written by the dynasty that replaced him.
cards.answerDate: Reignedc. 1075 – 1046 BCEDiedc. 1046 BCE, at Muye
cards.abstract:
King Zhou of Shang, whose own name was Di Xin, was the last king of the Shang dynasty and is the standard Chinese example of the tyrant who loses the Mandate of Heaven. He moved the capital to Zhaoge and spent his reign on expensive campaigns against the Renfang states to the east. Later tradition credits him with a lake filled with wine and a forest of trees hung with roast meat, with elaborate instruments of torture, and with being led into all of it by his consort Daji. He was defeated by King Wu of Zhou at the battle of Muye around 1046 BCE, and the accounts have him die by his own hand in the burning of his palace at the Deer Terrace. The name he is known by is not his: Zhou 紂 is a posthumous insult given him by his conquerors, meaning roughly a horse’s crupper strap.

Modern scholarship treats the atrocity stories with considerable caution. The Han sceptic Wang Chong already thought them unreliable, and the charges demonstrably grow in number and colour the further in time a source stands from the events. The contemporary bronzes and oracle bones, which are the only sources that are not Zhou propaganda, show a king performing his ritual duties much as his predecessors had. He matters to the history of tea only at second hand, because he is sometimes named as the king to whom the southwestern states sent tea as tribute in the eleventh century BCE. The source usually behind that story is the fourth-century Huayang Guozhi, which in fact describes Ba sending tea to his conqueror King Wu of Zhou, not to him.

cards.question: The longest-lasting Chinese dynasty, and the one during which Confucianism and Daoism appeared, was the _____, which held the Mandate of Heaven for nearly eight centuries.
cards.answerDate: Ruled1046 – 256 BCEEastern Zhoufrom 771 BCE
cards.abstract:
The Zhou dynasty overthrew the Shang at Muye in about 1046 BCE and lasted, in name at least, until 256 BCE, which makes it the longest dynasty in Chinese history. It is divided at 771 BCE, when the capital was moved east to Luoyang after a catastrophic defeat, into the Western and Eastern Zhou. The Zhou kings invented the Mandate of Heaven to justify their own seizure of power, and every later dynasty used the same argument in turn. Real power drained away from them after 771 BCE, and the Eastern Zhou is better known by the names of its two halves, the Spring and Autumn period and the Warring States. Those centuries of political collapse produced the richest philosophical argument in Chinese history, and Confucius, Laozi, Mozi, Mencius and Han Feizi all belong to them.

Buddhism arrived later, from India, but Confucianism and Daoism were both Eastern Zhou growths, and all three traditions would eventually take up tea. What they valued in it was not the taste, which by every account was frankly bitter, but its usefulness in medicine and in staying awake through long devotions. Zhou-era tea was a decoction rather than a beverage, described as heavy, thick and very bitter, and it was drunk for its effect rather than for any pleasure in it. It also stayed a southwestern product throughout the dynasty, because Sichuan and Yunnan lay about as far from Luoyang as it was possible to be and remain in the Chinese world. Only when the state of Qin conquered the southwest in 316 BCE did tea begin to move north in any quantity, and by then the Zhou kings were a formality with sixty years left to run.

cards.question: The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary, traditionally credited to the Duke of Zhou, is the _____, which explains the tea word jia as bitter tu.
cards.answerDate: Compiled4th – 2nd century BCEGuo Pu’s notesc. 310 CE
cards.abstract:
The Erya is the oldest Chinese dictionary to survive, and the only one of the Thirteen Classics that is a reference work rather than a text to be expounded. Joseph Needham placed its compilation between the late fourth and the early second centuries BCE, with some material older and some added as late as the first century BCE. Tradition credits it to the Duke of Zhou, or to Confucius, or to his disciples, but the book is plainly a compilation of glosses gathered from commentaries on pre-Qin texts. It runs to nineteen sections holding 2,094 entries and about 4,300 words, arranged by subject: kinship, buildings, utensils, the heavens, hills, waters, plants, trees, insects, fish, birds and beasts. Each section title begins with the word shi, meaning to explain, and the whole was the authoritative guide to the vocabulary of the classics throughout the Han.

Its entry on tea is short and has been quoted ever since: jia is bitter tu. The commentary of Guo Pu, written around 310 CE, expands that into a description of the plant and of what people did with it. Guo Pu says the plant is a small tree resembling a gardenia, that its winter leaves may be boiled to make a soup for drinking, that leaves gathered late are called ming, that another name is chuan, and that the people of Shu call it kutu. A soup is exactly what the phrasing suggests, and nothing in it implies a beverage of the kind a modern reader would recognise. The entry is nonetheless one of the earliest descriptions of the tea plant anywhere, and it puts cultivation squarely in the southwest.

cards.question: Zhang Yi’s dictionary of about 230 CE, the _____, carries the first surviving recipe telling a reader how to make and then brew a cake of tea.
cards.answerDate: Compiledc. 230 CEEntries2,343Renamed BoyaSui, 581 – 618 CE
cards.abstract:
The Guangya, the Broadened Erya, is a dictionary edited by Zhang Yi around 230 CE, during the Three Kingdoms period. Zhang modelled it deliberately on the Erya, keeping the same nineteen subject divisions and setting out to supply what four centuries had added since. On Wang Niansun’s standard Qing edition it holds 2,343 entries and 18,150 characters, roughly 5,000 entries more than the received Erya. Its botanical sections are the most original part: Zhang nearly doubled the plants and trees his model had covered, and most of those entries are new rather than repeated. It was later renamed the Boya, the Erya Expanded, because the character guang clashed with the personal name of Emperor Yang of Sui and so fell under a naming taboo.

Its passage on tea is the earliest practical account anyone has of how the leaf was actually made up and prepared for drinking. It says that in the country between Hubei and Sichuan the leaves are picked and made into cakes, and that cakes made of older leaves are bound with rice. To drink it, the cake is baked until it turns reddish, pounded to small pieces, put in a china pot and covered with boiling water, with onion, ginger and orange added. The drink, it adds, renders one sober after intoxication and keeps one awake, which are the two effects early Chinese writing on tea returns to most often. That is a soup rather than a cup of tea, but everything in it that matters is already there: compressed cakes, roasting, grinding, infusion in hot water, and a clear idea of what the stuff is for.

cards.question: For most of Chinese history tea travelled and was sold not loose but as _____, steamed and pressed into cakes, bricks or nuggets before drying.
cards.answerDate: Standard formTang and Song, 618 – 1279 CEDisplacedearly Ming, from 1391
cards.abstract:
Compressed tea is tea steamed and pressed into a solid block, cake, brick or nugget, then dried and often aged before sale. It was the normal form of tea in China from the earliest descriptions of manufacture until the Ming, and loose leaf is the historical newcomer. The reason is transport: a brick is compact, survives handling, and travels on a mule or a camel in a way that a basket of dry leaf does not. That made it the currency of the Tea Horse Road into Tibet and of the caravan routes into Mongolia and Siberia, where tea bricks were used as actual money into the twentieth century. Drinking it took three steps: toast a piece of the cake over the fire, grind it to powder, and whisk that powder into hot water.

The technique appears in China during the Han dynasty, and it was a considerable advance on what had gone before it. Steaming the leaves before drying and pressing them cut the bitterness and, more importantly, cut the spoilage, which had been ruinous when leaves were simply dried over charcoal fires. The Guangya of about 230 CE describes cakes of exactly this kind, bound together with rice when they were made from older and coarser leaves. Compressed tea stayed the standard form right through the Tang and the Song, which is why Lu Yu writes at length about roasting and grinding a cake and hardly at all about steeping a leaf. It survives today mainly in the post-fermented teas of Yunnan, in the dome-shaped tuocha and the disc-shaped bingcha, and in the bricks that are broken up for Tibetan butter tea.

cards.question: Tea became part of the discipline of _____, the Chinese meditation school known in Japan as Zen, whose monks needed to stay awake through long sittings.
cards.answerDate: Developedfrom the 6th century CEReached Japan13th century CE
cards.abstract:
Chan Buddhism is the Chinese school of Mahayana Buddhism that puts meditation at the centre of practice, and whose name comes from the Sanskrit dhyana, meaning meditative absorption. It developed in China from the sixth century CE onwards and reached its classic form under the Tang and Song. Tradition traces its lineage to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk placed in the late fifth century, though the records needed for a reliable account of early Chan do not survive. The Tang masters gave it the character it is now known for: the sixth patriarch Huineng, then Mazu Daoyi and Linji Yixuan, whose teaching was blunt, sudden and suspicious of book learning. From China it spread outward, south to Vietnam as Thien, north to Korea as Seon, and east to Japan in the thirteenth century as Zen.

Tea and this school fit together for a plain physiological reason, since a monk sitting in meditation for hours before dawn has a straightforward need to stay awake. Chinese Buddhism had valued the leaf long before Chan existed, as a medicine, as a remedy for thirst and fatigue, and as something to mix with other herbs. Monasteries were also unusually well placed to grow it, holding mountain land at exactly the altitudes tea prefers and having disciplined labour on hand to work it. A great many of the most celebrated Chinese teas began in temple gardens, and the monks of Mount Meng in Sichuan prepared the imperial tribute tea there for a thousand years. When Chan went to Japan as Zen the habit went with it, and the Japanese tea ceremony grew directly out of monastic practice.

cards.question: Chinese tradition puts the first deliberate planting of tea on _____ in Sichuan, where seven bushes are said to have been set between the five peaks.
cards.answerDate: Seven treesGanlu era, 53 – 50 BCETribute from724 CE
cards.abstract:
Mount Meng, Mengshan, is a mountain in Ya’an in western Sichuan, about 125 kilometres (78 miles) southwest of Chengdu, and Chinese tradition treats it as the birthplace of tea cultivation. The claim is specific and it is worth being clear about what it does and does not say. Tea had been gathered from wild trees for a long time before this; what Mount Meng is credited with is the deliberate planting and tending of it. The story attaches to a Daoist named Wu Lizhen, who is said to have planted seven tea bushes between the mountain’s five peaks during the Ganlu era of Emperor Xuan of Han, from 53 to 50 BCE. Cuttings taken from those seven are said to have stocked the rest of the mountain, and the spot where they stood is still shown to visitors.

Buddhist monasteries were established on the five peaks, and the mountain’s tea was picked and prepared by their monks. Mount Meng tea was named an imperial tribute in 724 CE and stayed one through the Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing, which is about as long a run as any tea has had. Each spring, from the Tang to the Qing, 360 leaves were picked and prepared by the monks for presentation to the emperor, and the tea was used in sacrifices to heaven and to the imperial ancestors. More than a thousand years of Chinese poetry and prose praise the mountain’s tea, which is unusual even by the standards of Chinese tea writing. Ya’an and neighbouring Qionglai are accordingly described in China as the birthplace of tea cultivation, and the region markets itself on exactly that claim.

cards.question: The Daoist credited with domesticating tea by planting seven bushes on Mount Meng in the first century BCE is _____, honoured a thousand years later by a Song emperor.
cards.answerDate: PlantedGanlu era, 53 – 50 BCEHonouredby Emperor Xiaozong, 1162 – 1189
cards.abstract:
Wu Lizhen is the figure Chinese tradition credits with turning tea from a plant that was gathered into a plant that was grown. He is described as a Daoist master, and he is placed on Mount Meng in Sichuan during the Ganlu era of Emperor Xuan of the Han, between 53 and 50 BCE. The story is that he planted seven tea bushes among the mountain’s five peaks and tended them until they were mature enough to take cuttings from. Those cuttings, in the telling, stocked the whole mountain and made it the first place in the world where tea was cultivated deliberately. The tea that came of those bushes was Mengding Ganlu, which grew so prized that it was reserved for the emperor and picked up a second name, the tea of the immortals.

Long afterwards Emperor Xiaozong of the Song gave Wu Lizhen the posthumous title Master of Ganlu, meaning sweet dew, and it is from that title that the tea takes its name. How much of any of this is history is another matter, and the honest answer is that none of it can be checked against a contemporary record. The details come from tradition rather than from any contemporary document, and versions of the story differ about who he was and where he got his plants. One popular retelling makes him a Buddhist returning from study in India with the cuttings, which sits oddly beside the Daoist of the older accounts. What is not in doubt is that the mountain has grown tea for a very long time, and that Chinese tea culture has treated his seven bushes as its own founding act for over a thousand years.

cards.question: The yellow-green Sichuan tea whose name means sweet dew, is _____, picked by monks and sent to the emperor every spring for the better part of a thousand years.
cards.answerDate: Named tribute724 CETribute untilQing, ended 1912
cards.abstract:
Mengding Ganlu is a green tea from Mount Meng in Sichuan, and its name means the sweet dew of Mengding, the top of Mount Meng. The name honours Wu Lizhen, the Daoist said to have planted the mountain’s first seven tea bushes, who was posthumously titled Master of Ganlu by Emperor Xiaozong of the Song. The finished leaf is a yellowish green and the liquor is delicate, with a sweetness in the aftertaste that the name plays on. It has a long association with the Buddhist monasteries built on the mountain’s five peaks, whose monks did both the picking and the making of it for centuries on end. Every spring, from the Tang dynasty to the Qing, 360 leaves were prepared there and sent to the emperor.

It was also called Xian Cha, the tea of the immortals, a name that says a great deal about how the tea was regarded and nothing whatever about the leaf itself. Mount Meng tea was entered on the tribute list in 724 CE and stayed on it under five successive dynasties, which is an unusually long career even for a famous Chinese tea. That is the pattern nearly every celebrated Chinese tea follows, in which a reputation begins with the imperial court and then spreads outward from it to everybody else. The physician Li Shizhen singled it out in the Ming as warm in nature and able to take charge of disease, unlike most teas, which Chinese medicine classes as cooling. The mountain also produces yellow teas, among them Mengding Huangya and Mengding Shihua, made from the same gardens by a different process.

cards.question: The Bronze Age kingdom of the Chengdu plain, whose masked bronzes were dug up at Sanxingdui, was _____, conquered by Qin in 316 BCE.
cards.answerDate: Sanxingduic. 2050 – 1250 BCEKaiming kingsfrom 666 BCEConquered316 BCE
cards.abstract:
Shu was the ancient kingdom of the western Sichuan basin, centred on the Chengdu plain and reaching northeast towards the upper Han River. Its archaeology is spectacular and largely unexpected: the site of Sanxingdui, 40 kilometres (25 miles) north of Chengdu, was the centre of a substantial Bronze Age kingdom from roughly 2050 to 1250 BCE. The bronze masks and figures found there look nothing like the ritual vessels of the contemporary Shang, which is a useful corrective to any account of Bronze Age China written around the Yellow River alone. Its early rulers are semi-legendary, among them Cancong, whose name means silkworm bush, Boguan the cypress irrigator and Duyu the cuckoo. A man named Bieling, from Chu, founded the Kaiming line in 666 BCE, and it lasted twelve generations.

Shu fell to Qin in 316 BCE, after a quarrel within the ruling house drew Qin in, and the general Sima Cuo defeated the last Kaiming king near the Jialing River. Qin turned the kingdom into a commandery, threw an enormous wall around Chengdu and redistributed the farmland into rectangular plots on the Qin pattern. What Qin acquired along with the land was tea, and with it the accumulated local knowledge of how to grow the plant and what to do with the leaf. Every one of the early Chinese names for tea is credited to the people of Shu and Ba, and Guo Pu’s note on the Erya says in so many words that the people of Shu call it kutu. The southwest had been outside the reach of any northern government until then, which is much of why tea took so long to become a Chinese rather than a Sichuanese habit.

cards.question: The confederation of eastern Sichuan whose rulers are said to have sent tea north as tribute to King Wu of Zhou was _____, absorbed by Qin in 316 BCE.
cards.answerDate: Tribute to King Wuc. 1046 BCECapitalJiangzhou, from c. 4th c. BCEAbsorbed316 BCE
cards.abstract:
Ba occupied eastern Sichuan, and was less a centralised state than a loose confederation of chiefdoms that absorbed a number of distinct peoples. Its capital moved repeatedly under pressure from Chu and settled at Jiangzhou, on the site of modern Chongqing. It traded and intermarried with Chu, supplied mercenaries to the Chu army, and bordered Shu and Qin through the Warring States period. Its distinctive war dance, the Ba Yu, performed with weapons and sung in the Ba language, was still being staged at the Chinese court in the Tang, more than a thousand years after the state itself had gone. In 316 BCE Ba joined Qin in attacking Shu, and Qin turned on its ally the moment Shu had fallen, captured the last Ba king and made the territory a commandery.

Ba matters to tea because of a passage in the Huayang Guozhi, a history of the southwest written by Chang Qu in the fourth century CE. It describes the rulers of Ba sending red lacquer, honey and tea north as tribute to King Wu of Zhou, which places tea at about 1046 BCE. The same account has the southwest sending copper, iron, salt, cinnabar, preserved fish, timber, hemp and herbs, with good tea from the hills of Shifang and rare tea from Nanan and Wuyang. The obvious caution applies to all of it, since the Huayang Guozhi was written some fourteen centuries after the events it is reporting on. It is nonetheless the earliest claim of tea being sent north at all, and the earliest documented tribute tea is far later, a gift of a thousand jin presented by Wen Jiao in the fourth century CE.

cards.question: The ruler who took the title First Emperor in 221 BCE was _____, born decades after the Qin conquest of the southwest that first brought tea within reach of the north.
cards.answerDate: Born259 BCEFirst Emperorfrom 221 BCEDied210 BCE
cards.abstract:
Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng in 259 BCE, became king of Qin as a child and in 221 BCE completed the conquest of the remaining Warring States. He took a new title for the new situation, huangdi, rendered in English as emperor, and called himself the First Emperor. His government standardised the script, the currency, the axle widths of carts and the weights and measures, and replaced the old aristocratic holdings with commanderies run by appointees. He is remembered about equally for the terracotta army guarding his tomb near Xi’an and for the burning of books and the burying of scholars attributed to his reign. He died in 210 BCE while touring the east, hunting for an elixir of immortality, and his dynasty outlasted him by four years.

The conquest that actually mattered for tea happened before he was born, and the point is worth making plainly, because popular accounts regularly hand him the credit for it. Qin took Shu and Ba in 316 BCE, under King Huiwen and his general Sima Cuo, 56 years before Ying Zheng was born. That conquest gave a northern power its first real grip on the southwest, and with it the tea trees and the knowledge of how to work them. What unification then did was to remove the frontiers between Sichuan and the Yellow River valley, so that goods, people and customs could travel the length of the empire. Tea moved north slowly along those roads, still bitter and still mostly a medicine, but for the first time reaching the cities of the Yellow River and the central plain in any quantity at all.

cards.question: Chen Shou’s _____, compiled in the third century CE, is the standard source for its period and carries an early notice of tea drunk in place of wine.
cards.answerDate: Compiled3rd century CEPeriod covered184 – 280 CE
cards.abstract:
The Records of the Three Kingdoms, the Sanguozhi, is the authoritative history of the three states that divided China after the Han collapsed. Chen Shou compiled it in the third century CE, within living memory of the events, which is unusually close for a Chinese standard history. It is arranged in three books for the three states, Wei, Shu Han and Wu, and is built out of annals and biographies in the manner Sima Qian established. Chen Shou served the Jin, whose founding family had taken power from Wei, and that allegiance colours which of the three states he treats as the legitimate successor to the Han. In the fifth century Pei Songzhi annotated it heavily, quoting dozens of works that no longer exist, and the commentary is now as valuable as the text.

The book is also one of the small handful of pre-Tang sources that mention tea at all, which is why it turns up in histories of the drink so far out of its subject. In the biography of the Wu official Wei Zhao it records that he could not manage the quantity of wine his king expected at banquets, and was quietly served tea instead. That is the origin of the phrase yi cha dai jiu, to substitute tea for wine, which is still said in China today when someone at a table does not drink. The passage is worth more than its length suggests, because it shows tea already familiar enough at a southern court to be an accepted substitute at a formal occasion. It is not a picture of a pleasant drink, though, and everything else known about third-century tea says it was still a bitter and largely medicinal one.

cards.question: The Wu historian excused from his king’s drinking and served tea instead was _____, who was executed for refusing to rewrite the history he was compiling.
cards.answerDate: Born204 CEDied273 CE
cards.abstract:
Wei Zhao was an official, scholar and historian of the state of Eastern Wu, born in 204 CE. He held senior posts including Prefect of the Grand Clerks and Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, and he was chief editor of the Book of Wu, the state’s official history. He appears in the Sanguozhi under the name Wei Yao, because Chen Shou altered the character to avoid the personal name of Sima Zhao, father of the founder of the Jin dynasty. He had taught the father of the last Wu emperor, Sun Hao, which bought him a certain licence at court. It did not buy him enough, and when Sun Hao ordered him to alter parts of the history he refused, on the ground that it would violate the principle of the thing, and was put to death in 273 CE.

The episode tea historians know him for belongs to the same court and says something about the same temperament. Sun Hao set a compulsory minimum of wine for every guest at his frequent banquets, and Wei Zhao, whose constitution was weak, had no hope of drinking anything like it. His biography records that the king let him off, and that he took tea instead, either openly or discreetly poured into his cup in place of the wine. It is one of the earliest datable references anywhere to a person drinking tea on a social occasion rather than swallowing it as a medicine, and it is a single line in a biography. His tomb and a memorial temple still stand at Danyang in Jiangsu, which is a respectable afterlife for a man killed over a paragraph.

cards.question: The last ruler of Eastern Wu, whose banquets carried a compulsory wine ration, was _____, the grandson of Sun Quan who surrendered to Jin in 280 CE.
cards.answerDate: Reigned264 – 280 CESurrendered280 CEDied284 CE
cards.abstract:
Sun Hao was the fourth and last emperor of Eastern Wu, reigning from 264 to 280 CE. He was a grandson of Sun Quan, the founder of the state, and came to the throne when the court passed over the previous emperor’s children. He began well enough, releasing palace women, distributing grain and relieving the poor, and the histories then have him deteriorate quite rapidly into cruelty, extravagance and very heavy drinking. Those histories were written under the dynasty that destroyed him, which is a caution worth carrying, though the picture of him is consistent across sources. Jin armies came down the Yangtze and took Wu in 280 CE, ending the Three Kingdoms period altogether, and he lived out four more years as a marquis in the Jin capital.

His banquets are the whole of the reason he appears in any history of tea, and the detail is preserved by accident rather than design. He required every guest to drink a set quantity of wine, and the courtier Wei Zhao, who had taught his father and could not manage it, was permitted tea in its place. The Sanguozhi records the arrangement in Wei Zhao’s own biography, and it is among the earliest notices anywhere of tea being drunk in company rather than taken as a remedy. The indulgence did not last, and Sun Hao later had Wei Zhao put to death in 273 CE for refusing to alter passages of the official history he was compiling. The custom outlived both of them, and yi cha dai jiu, substituting tea for wine, is still what a Chinese host offers a guest who will not drink.

cards.question: The practice of sending a district’s finest leaf to the emperor for his own use is called _____, and nearly every famous Chinese tea began its reputation as one.
cards.answerDate: Earliest record4th century CETribute worksChangxing, from 700 CE
cards.abstract:
Tribute tea, gongcha, is tea sent to the emperor as an obligation rather than sold, and for most of Chinese history it was how a tea made its name. The court could not drink anything like the quantity that arrived, so the surplus was distributed among officials, who shared it with their families and friends. A village that supplied the emperor acquired a reputation that spread outward through exactly that network, and its tea commanded a price to match. The earliest documented instance is from the Jin period, when the dignitary Wen Jiao presented the throne with a thousand jin of tea. Earlier claims exist, including the Huayang Guozhi’s account of Ba sending tea to King Wu of Zhou, but that source is fourth-century CE and the event it describes is eleventh-century BCE.

By the fifth century the practice is clearly established in the written record, and under the Tang there were seventeen places in the empire producing tea for the court. Under the Liu Song, the first of the southern dynasties and no relation to the later Song, it was written that a mountain near Wuchang grew tea reserved for the emperor. In 700 CE dedicated tribute works were founded around Changxing and Yixing, and the ones on Mount Guzhu grew into more than thirty workshops staffed by a thousand corvée labourers and more. Mount Meng in Sichuan was named a tribute source in 724 CE and stayed one under five dynasties, with 360 leaves prepared by its monks each spring. The system pushed quality upward and distorted it at the same time, because a garden growing for a single customer ends up growing precisely what that customer has come to expect.

cards.question: The short dynasty that reunified China in 589 CE and is the _____, taken by convention as the point at which tea turns from a medicine into a drink.
cards.answerDate: Ruled581 – 618 CEReunified China589 CE
cards.abstract:
The Sui dynasty held China for thirty-seven years, from 581 to 618 CE, and reunified the country in 589 after nearly three centuries of division. Yang Jian, known as Emperor Wen, took the throne in the north and then conquered the southern Chen, ending the period of the Northern and Southern Dynasties. The dynasty built the Grand Canal, rebuilt the examination system, recodified the law and reorganised the granaries, and exhausted itself doing so. It collapsed under his son in a revolt touched off by ruinous campaigns in Korea, and the Tang took over in 618 CE. Its importance is wildly out of proportion to its length, because the Tang inherited a unified state with most of the institutions it would need already built and paid for.

For the history of tea the Sui is the conventional dividing line, and it is a line drawn by hindsight rather than by anything that happened in those thirty-seven years. Nearly four centuries had passed since the Three Kingdoms, and across them the handling of the leaf had improved to the point where drinking it was a pleasure rather than a treatment. The reunification also joined the tea-growing south to the northern cities inside one political system, with a canal running between them capable of moving bulk goods in quantity. What had not changed was the form of the thing, and tea remained a matter of compressed cakes, roasted and ground and whisked into hot water, for several centuries more. It was under the Tang that followed that tea came fully of age, acquired a literature of its own in Lu Yu, and began to reach the countries around China.
